title: Take-home assignments strategy
summary: Plan, scope, and deliver take-home coding challenges that read clearly, run cleanly, and show how you actually think.
objectives: Read the brief carefully and clarify scope before writing any code
Time-box the work and prioritise a working end-to-end solution
Structure the repo so a reviewer can run it in minutes
Write a README that explains decisions, trade-offs, and how to run
Add a few meaningful tests instead of chasing full coverage
Document assumptions and what you would do with more time
Avoid common red flags that get strong candidates rejected

quiz.q: What is the single most important thing a reviewer wants from your take-home?
options: Code that runs and solves the core problem clearly
quiz.why: Reviewers first check that it runs and solves the stated problem cleanly. Clarity beats cleverness and volume.

quiz.q: You have a strict time-box but cannot finish every feature. What should you do?
options: Submit nothing until it is perfect
Deliver a working core and note remaining work in the README
Hand in broken half-features for each requirement
Ask for a deadline extension every time
quiz.why: A working end-to-end slice plus an honest 'what I'd do with more time' section is far stronger than several half-finished features.

quiz.q: Why should you write a README even for a small take-home?
options: So the reviewer can run it and understand your decisions quickly
quiz.why: The README is the first thing a reviewer reads. Clear setup steps and stated trade-offs make their job easy and signal seniority.

quiz.q: A brief is ambiguous about an input format. What is the best response?
quiz.answer: State a reasonable assumption explicitly in the README (and ask the recruiter if there's time), then build to it.
quiz.why: Reviewers want to see judgement. Documenting an explicit, reasonable assumption is better than guessing silently or stalling.

quiz.q: Name two things to check before you submit, beyond 'the code works'.
quiz.answer: That it runs from a clean clone (fresh setup), and that no secrets or API keys are committed.
quiz.why: A clean-clone run and removing secrets are classic last-mile checks. A repo that fails on a fresh machine reads as careless.

quiz.q: Should you aim for 100% test coverage on a take-home?
options: No — a few meaningful tests on core logic are enough
quiz.why: Time is limited. A handful of well-chosen tests on the important paths shows discipline; chasing total coverage usually wastes the time-box.

resources.label: The Pragmatic Programmer (Hunt & Thomas) — on clarity and trade-offs

body_markdown:
## What reviewers actually grade

A take-home is not a puzzle to win — it's a small sample of how you'd work on the team. Reviewers spend ten to twenty minutes per submission, so they look for the same things every time: does it **run**, does it **solve the stated problem**, and can they **follow your reasoning**.

Clarity beats cleverness. A simple, readable solution that runs from a clean clone will out-score a brilliant but tangled one. Most rejections come from repos that don't run, ignore the brief, or hide good work behind no explanation.

## Scope before you code

Read the brief twice. List the **must-haves** versus the **nice-to-haves**. If anything is ambiguous, write down a reasonable assumption (and email the recruiter if there's time). Then time-box: decide up front how many hours this gets, and aim for a working end-to-end slice first.

A common trap is starting four features and finishing none. Finish one path completely, then widen.

## Structure the repo for the reviewer

Make it runnable in minutes. Pin dependencies, give one obvious entry point, and put setup steps at the top of the README.

```bash
git clone <your-repo> && cd <your-repo>
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python main.py --input data/sample.csv
```

Keep secrets out of the repo. Read keys from environment variables, never commit them, and add a `.env.example` showing what's needed.

## A small, honest test suite

You don't need full coverage — you need to show you can test the parts that matter. Pick the core logic and the trickiest edge case.

```python
from analyse import top_tag

def test_top_tag_picks_most_common():
    rows = [{"tag": "a"}, {"tag": "b"}, {"tag": "a"}]
    assert top_tag(rows) == "a"

def test_top_tag_empty_returns_none():
    assert top_tag([]) is None
```

Run them with `pytest -q` and make sure they pass on a clean checkout.

## If the task involves an LLM

Some modern take-homes ask you to call a model. Keep it simple, keep the key in an environment variable, and use the current Claude Messages API — not any deprecated completions endpoint.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this ticket in one line."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Note in the README which model you chose and why, and handle the case where the key is missing so the grader gets a clear error, not a crash.

## Final checklist and your task

Before you submit: clone fresh and run it, check no secrets are committed, proofread the README, and write a short 'with more time I would...' section. Then ship it on time.

Your task: take any small script from this course, wrap it in a clean repo with a README, one entry point, and two tests, exactly as if it were a take-home.

slides.title: Take-home assignments strategy
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month Six, where we get you ready to apply and interview. In this lesson we tackle the take-home assignment, the coding challenge many companies send before they talk to you. By the end you'll know how to scope it, structure it, and deliver something that makes a reviewer say yes.

slides.title: What reviewers grade
bullets: Does it run from a clean clone?
Does it solve the stated problem?
slides.narration: First, understand what's being graded. A reviewer spends maybe ten to twenty minutes on your submission. They check three things: does it actually run, does it solve the problem in the brief, and can they follow how you got there. Clear and simple always beats clever and tangled.

slides.title: Scope before you code
slides.narration: Before writing a single line, read the brief twice. List what's required versus what's optional. If something is unclear, write down a reasonable assumption and, if there's time, ask the recruiter. Then decide how many hours this gets. Discipline here is what separates strong candidates.

slides.title: Finish one path first
slides.narration: The biggest trap is starting four features and finishing none. Instead, build one complete path from input to output, get it working, then widen. A small solution that runs end to end beats a sprawling one that's broken in five places.

slides.title: Make it run in minutes
bullets: Setup steps at top of README.
slides.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python main.py --input data/sample.csv
slides.narration: Structure the repo so a reviewer can run it fast. Pin your dependencies in a requirements file, give one clear entry point, and put the exact setup commands at the top of the README. If they can clone and run in two minutes, you've already won points.

slides.title: Keep secrets out
bullets: Never commit a key or token.
slides.code:
import os
key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
# never: key = "sk-ant-..."
slides.narration: A classic rejection is committing an A P I key or a password. Always read secrets from environment variables, never hard-code them, and never commit them. Add a dot env example file that lists the variables needed without the real values. This shows you understand basic security hygiene.

slides.title: A small, honest test suite
bullets: Test the core logic and one tricky case.
Make sure they pass on a clean checkout.
slides.narration: You don't need one hundred percent coverage. Pick the core logic and the trickiest edge case, and write a few clear tests for those. Run them with pytest and confirm they pass on a fresh checkout. A handful of meaningful tests signals discipline far better than chasing every line.

slides.title: If the task uses an L L M
bullets: Keep the key in an env var.
Say which model you chose and why.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Some take-homes ask you to call a model. Use the current Claude Messages A P I, not any deprecated completions endpoint. Keep your key in an environment variable, and in the README say which model you picked and why. Handle a missing key gracefully so the grader sees a clear message, not a crash.

slides.title: Write the README
bullets: What you'd do with more time.
slides.narration: The README is the first thing the reviewer reads, so make it count. Explain how to run it, the decisions and trade-offs you made, any assumptions, and a short section on what you'd improve with more time. This is where you turn working code into a story about how you think.

slides.title: Last-mile checks
slides.narration: Before you submit, do the last-mile checks. Clone the repo into a fresh folder and run it like the reviewer will. Confirm no secrets slipped in. Proofread the README for typos. And then ship it on time, because a late submission undoes a lot of good work.
